newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro court raps Belgium in media freedom case.
newsitem.headline: Euro court raps Belgium in media freedom case.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights ruled on Monday that Belgium deprived two journalists of freedom of expression by convicting them of defaming judges in a child custody case.

The court ordered Belgium to pay damages and legal costs to editor Leo de Haes and reporter Hugo Gijsels, both of the weekly magazine Humo, over articles they published in 1986 including one entitled "Incest is permitted in Flanders".

The judges at the Strasbourg-based court voted by seven to two that Belgium violated their rights to freedom of expression and voted unanimously that Belgium had deprived the two men of a fair trial on defamation charges.

A Belgian court convicted them in 1988 of defaming three judges and an Advocate-General of the Antwerp court of appeal who awarded custody of two boys to a Belgian notary in a divorce case even though the notary's wife accused him of sexually abusing the children, aged six and three.
The Humo articles alleged the Belgian judges were unfairly biased in favour of the notary, saying the judges and the notary shared sympathy with an extreme right-wing group.

"The accusations in question amounted to an opinion, whose truth, by definition, was not susceptible of proof," the European Court said. It also said the criticisms seemed justified by the information Humo had obtained about the case.

"Although Mr De Haes and Mr Gijsels' comments were without doubt severely critical, they nevertheless appeared proportionate to the stir and indignation caused by the matters alleged in their articles," it said.
At their 1988 trial the journalists were barred from presenting evidence from experts about the children's state of health that could have bolstered their case.
They were fined a symbolic franc (three U.S. cents) in a verdict upheld by a 1990 appeal and ordered to pay for publication of the judgment against them.

The damages awarded on Monday by the court, a branch of the 40-nation Council of Europe, would match the cost of publication. The court also awarded the two legal costs of 851,697 Belgian francs ($24,690).
